headline: Three lint verbs, and each is short because the parser that feeds it is strict.
summary: `pki.lint.cms`, `pki.lint.tsp` and `pki.lint.attrcert` complete the lint surface, covering RFC 5652 messages, RFC 3161 timestamp tokens and RFC 5755 attribute certificates. Each profile carries a handful of rows rather than a table of them, because this toolkit's strict parsers already refuse most of what those documents require: a clause refused at parse reaches an operator as `lint/unparseable` carrying the parser's own code, and a rule for it would be a branch no input can drive. Every clause left without a row has a conformance vector asserting that verdict instead.

Added: `pki.lint.cms(pem | der | parsed, opts?)` lints a CMS ContentInfo against the RFC 5652 profile, under `profile: "rfc5652"`. A content type this parser reads that is not signed-data carries no signerInfos, so every row is not applicable to it rather than reported against it. A content type the parser does not read, which includes id-data, arrives as a single fatal `lint/unparseable` carrying the parser's own code.

Its rows are what the parser leaves: a signing-time naming a year from 1950 to 2049 encoded as GeneralizedTime where section 11.3 requires UTCTime, a signer whose digest algorithm the digestAlgorithms set does not list, which section 5.1 has list the digests every signer employs and so covers a countersigner's digest as well, a version 1 attribute certificate in the certificates field, and two notices, a SignedData carrying no signers and a detached signature whose content a verifier must be handed separately. The other direction of section 11.3 cannot be broken at all: a UTCTime carries two year digits that the clause reads as 19YY or 20YY, so every one of them names a year inside the window.

The signing-time rule reads the message's own signers and the countersignatures section 11.4 places in an unsigned attribute, including any nested inside those. A rule about a signed attribute governs one wherever it appears, so a signer cannot put the shape the clause forbids inside a countersignature and escape it. An encapsulated content that is itself a CMS message is linted by running the verb on that message, the way the certificates a message carries are linted with `pki.lint.certificate`. The finding names the message's own signer and says whether the attribute sat on a countersignature under it, rather than a position in that walk, which would send a reader to a different signer. Two digest identifiers naming the same algorithm are compared as RFC 5754 section 2 requires: absent parameters and an explicit NULL are the same digest, so a set that writes one beside a signer that writes the other is listing that signer's algorithm.

`pki.lint.tsp(pem | der, opts?)` lints an RFC 3161 timestamp token under `profile: "rfc3161"`. Its rows are a tsa hint naming a subject the token's own certificate does not carry, a serial number wider than the 160 bits a conforming consumer must accommodate, and a token stating no accuracy. The tsa row resolves which certificate verifies the token from the hash the ESS SigningCertificate or SigningCertificateV2 signed attribute carries, which names one certificate and which section 2.4.2 requires every token to hold. Either attribute answers: the original one carries no hash algorithm and RFC 2634 section 5.4 implies SHA-1 for it, so a token written that way resolves its signer as a v2 one does. RFC 5035 section 4 fixes no set of algorithms for the v2 attribute's hashAlgorithm, so the row reads a certHash under any digest this build computes, at the output lengths RFC 8702 section 2 fixes for id-shake128 and id-shake256. That hash says which of the certificates a token already carries the token names, which is a different question from whether a binding is strong enough to trust, and `pki.tsp.verify` keeps its own narrower set for the latter. The SignerInfo identifier is not that fact: an issuer with a serial number, and a subject key identifier, are both values an issuer wrote, two certificates can carry either, and the certificate set a token embeds sits outside the token's signature, so a hint read against the first identifier match is a hint read against whichever certificate the sender put first. A token whose signer certificate is not embedded is passed over, to be supplied out of band. Carrying one certificate is not the same fact as carrying the signer's, since a token may embed an intermediate, and comparing a hint against that would report a conforming token. The clause says subject names, plural, so the row reads the subject and every subjectAltName entry alike. A distinguished name is compared under the RFC 5280 section 7.1 rules wherever it appears, since two encodings of one name are one name, a DNS name and the text of a mailbox and a URI are compared without regard to ASCII case, since DER canonicalizes the encoding and not the letters, and every other form is compared as its exact encoding, since a structured name such as an otherName is not settled by comparing decoded values.

`pki.lint.attrcert(pem | der, opts?)` lints an X.509 attribute certificate under `profile: "rfc5755"`. Its rows are the criticality each clause fixes for the extensions the profile defines, section 4.3's six and the ProxyInfo of section 7.2, a critical extension the profile does not define, a Holder naming more than one of its three options, a Holder entityName carrying more than one name where section 4.2.2 asks for one, a Holder baseCertificateID issuerUID, and an issuerUniqueID. The last two are permitted only where another certificate carries the matching field, so each is a warning naming that condition rather than an error. Section 4.2.2's requirements that these bytes DO settle are refused at parse instead, so they reach an operator as the parser's own code: a Holder baseCertificateID whose issuer is anything other than one non-empty directoryName is refused, which section 4.2.2 requires in the same words section 4.2.3 uses for the issuer. The remaining clauses of that section describe the public-key certificate the Holder names rather than the attribute certificate, so no row can answer them. What counts as outside the profile is membership in that set rather than whether this toolkit can decode the value: the attribute certificate decoder also reads AAControls, which section 7.4 places in a CA or AC issuer public-key certificate rather than in an attribute certificate.

`pki.lint.rules()` and `pki.lint.rules(profile, artifact)` reach the three new sets, with `"cms"`, `"tsp"` and `"attrcert"` joining the artifacts a profile name can be read under. `pki.lint.profiles()` lists the three beside the others, and now enumerates the same registry the verbs dispatch on, so a profile a verb can run is one that call answers with.

A fuzz target for each of the three, holding the contract every lint verb holds: hostile bytes return a report and never raise. Each drives the raw bytes at the ingestion boundary, splices them over a well-framed structure so the rules run on attacker-controlled values, and then puts them in each attribute or extension a rule reads a value out of.
Fixed: `pki.lint.tsp` compares a tsa hint against each form of name under the RFC 5280 section 7 rule for that form. A mailbox matches when its local part matches exactly and its host part matches without regard to ASCII case (section 7.5), and two URIs are prepared as section 7.4 requires, which lowercases the scheme and host, normalizes percent-encoding and path segments, and drops a default port for the ldap, http, https and ftp schemes that clause names, before the exact match it then calls for. Before, the whole value was folded to lowercase for both forms, so a hint differing from every name the certificate carries in a mailbox local part or a URI path read as one of them and went unreported. A dNSName is unchanged: section 7.2 makes the whole name case-insensitive. A hint in a form neither rule can read is passed over rather than reported, which is the verdict the row already gives where the signer's certificate is absent.

`pki.cms.decrypt` reads RFC 4055 section 4.1's OAEP defaults as the values that section assigns rather than inferring one from another. An absent `maskGenFunc` names mgf1SHA1, so a parameter set whose `hashFunc` is SHA-256 and whose `maskGenFunc` is omitted is the same set as one that writes MGF1-SHA-1 out, and both are now refused with `cms/unsupported-algorithm`. Before, the rule that the two hashes must agree was applied to the spelled-out form and skipped when the field was omitted, so a sender could step around it by leaving a field out. A set whose fields do agree, including one that omits `maskGenFunc` beside a SHA-1 `hashFunc`, still decrypts.

`pki.inspect` renders an IPv6 address in the form RFC 5952 fixes, lowercase with the longest run of zero groups compressed, wherever it appears. A subjectAltName entry and an RFC 3779 address block carrying the same octets now read the same; before, the first printed `2001:DB8:0:0:0:0:0:1` where the second printed `2001:db8::1`, so one report could show one address two ways. A name constraint's address and mask is still written as both halves joined by a slash, since that pair is not an address.

`pki.schema.x509.parse`, `pki.schema.cms.parse` and every other parser that reads an AlgorithmIdentifier refuse a present parameters field on nine identifiers whose specification says to omit it: `ecdsaWithSHA1`, `ecdsaWithSHA256`, `ecdsaWithSHA384`, `ecdsaWithSHA512` and `dsaWithSha1` (RFC 3279 sections 2.2.2 and 2.2.3, RFC 5758 section 3.2), and `shake128`, `shake256`, `id-RSASSA-PSS-SHAKE128` and `id-RSASSA-PSS-SHAKE256` (RFC 8702 sections 2, 3.1 and 3.2). The verdict is `<domain>/bad-algorithm-parameters`. The ECDSA and SHAKE shapes were already refused, a layer later and under a less specific code; they are now refused where the encoding is read. An identifier whose specification requires the field PRESENT and NULL, which is every `*WithRSAEncryption` and `rsaEncryption` itself under RFC 4055, is unaffected.
Changed: Each of the three verbs refuses a profile name belonging to another one by name, the way the existing verbs do, rather than running a certificate's rows against a message.

`pki.cms.countersign` adds the countersigner's digest algorithm to the SignedData `digestAlgorithms` set. RFC 5652 section 5.1 has that set list the digests every signer employs so a consumer can process the message in one pass, and section 11.4 makes a countersignature a SignerInfo. Whether the digest is already listed is decided by RFC 5754 section 2, under which absent parameters and an explicit NULL are one algorithm, so a message whose producer wrote the NULL spelling does not gain a second entry for the digest it already lists. The set is covered by no signature in the message, so every signature a countersigned message already carried still verifies.

`pki.attrcert.sign` writes an `aaControls` extension non-critical, where it wrote it critical before, and accepts a pre-encoded one at either criticality. RFC 5755 section 7.4 calls AAControls a PKC extension "intended to be used in CA and AC issuer PKCs" and fixes no criticality for an attribute certificate, so section 4.2.9 governs it there: an extension outside section 4.3 conforms when it is non-critical and does not when it is critical. An attribute certificate carrying a critical one is still refused at `pki.attrcert.verify`, and `pki.lint.attrcert` reports it.

`pki.attrcert.verify` compares a `uniformResourceIdentifier` target under RFC 5280 section 7.4, where it compared the two values as written before. A caller naming a target whose scheme case, default port, dot segment or percent-encoded unreserved character differs from the one the attribute certificate carries now matches it, which the clause's five preparation steps make the same URI. A target differing anywhere the clause leaves case-sensitive, a path among them, is still refused.

`pki.schema.attrcert.decodeExtension` cites RFC 5755 section 7.2 for the criticality it fixes for `acProxying`, where it cited section 7.3 before. Section 7.2 is Proxying; section 7.3 is the use of ObjectDigestInfo. The same call no longer states a fixed criticality for `aaControls`, because no clause fixes one.
